expect.statement: Randomized evidence on antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis, as identified by a systematic review and network meta-analysis with searches to June 2020, consists of six small, short (21 to 42 days), single-site trials with 395 participants in Thailand, Iran and China, mostly inpatients and mostly men, each comparing two of six antipsychotics (aripiprazole, haloperidol, olanzapine, paliperidone extended-release, quetiapine, risperidone); none had a placebo or no-medication arm, and two are titled as trials in amphetamine psychosis. Each trial reported no significant difference between its two drugs on the main psychotic symptoms, and the trials were too small to show that the drugs work equally well. Chaining the trials through their shared drugs, the network meta-analysis estimated lower symptom scores at the end of treatment on olanzapine (standardized mean difference −1.09, 95% CI −1.89 to −0.28) and quetiapine (−0.86, −1.61 to −0.11) than on risperidone, and higher scores on aripiprazole than on four of the other drugs (the review compared end-of-treatment scores, not changes from baseline); these are indirect estimates only, rated low certainty by the authors because data came partly from open-label trials and the trials differ in participants and design, and both advantages over risperidone rest on one open-label trial of haloperidol against risperidone with 44 participants. Dropout did not differ, but its intervals were too wide to be informative. Because no trial had a placebo arm, these trials cannot show whether antipsychotics speed recovery beyond what abstinence alone achieves; the one placebo-controlled trial the review found, of aripiprazole in people whose psychotic symptoms had already subsided, was excluded. Side effects were not pooled; as narrative reviews describe it, the one trial included in a 2009 Cochrane review found fewer extrapyramidal side effects on olanzapine than on haloperidol. Two narrative reviews state that acute psychosis usually resolves with abstinence alone, citing early studies of amphetamine psychosis published between 1958 and 1980 or an online clinical reference entry. How often psychosis persists after stopping is described in section 9.
expect.plain: A 2021 review found only six small trials, about 400 people in all, testing medicines for meth psychosis, always one medicine against another, never against a dummy pill. No trial found a clear difference between its two medicines; indirect comparisons favouring some medicines are uncertain. None of these trials tested whether the medicines help more than stopping meth alone.
expect.population: Adults with methamphetamine psychosis (two trials are titled as amphetamine psychosis), mostly inpatients and men, in trials in Thailand, Iran and China
expect.outcome: Severity of psychotic symptoms after 3 to 6 weeks; dropout; side effects (narrative reviews only)
expect.magnitude: Six head-to-head randomized trials (searches to June 2020), 395 participants, 42 to 120 per trial, 21 to 42 days; no placebo arm. Network estimates against risperidone, main symptoms at the end of treatment (SMD of final values, not of change scores): olanzapine −1.09 (−1.89 to −0.28) and quetiapine −0.86 (−1.61 to −0.11), indirect only; haloperidol −0.60 (−1.20 to 0.01), paliperidone extended-release −0.33 (−0.69 to 0.03) and aripiprazole 0.27 (−0.13 to 0.68), direct. Aripiprazole against olanzapine 1.36 (0.46 to 2.26), quetiapine 1.13 (0.28 to 1.98), haloperidol 0.87 (0.14 to 1.60) and paliperidone extended-release 0.60 (0.06 to 1.14), indirect. No direct comparison significant. Dropout odds ratios against risperidone 0.18 to 2.77, every interval including 1. Authors' GRADE: low or very low for every estimate.
expect.grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence, now read through a systematic review and network meta-analysis (Srisurapanont et al., 2021; AMSTAR 2 low confidence on the first reading), so the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews; the six trial reports themselves have not been read. Starts high. Risk of bias −1: two of the six trials were open-label (high risk in two domains) and allocation concealment was unclear in four; both indirect advantages over risperidone, and three of the four against aripiprazole, are chained through the open-label haloperidol–risperidone pilot trial (44 participants). Indirectness −1: the network is a chain without a closed loop, so every indirect estimate rests on transitivity, which the authors themselves doubt (participants and designs differ); two trials are titled as amphetamine psychosis; and active-comparator trials cannot address benefit beyond abstinence, the claim's open question. Imprecision −2: 42 to 120 participants per trial, every direct comparison's interval includes no difference, and dropout odds ratios have intervals as wide as 0.00 to 218. Inconsistency not downgraded, though it can hardly be judged: the global I² of 0% for main symptoms rests on one degree of freedom (six two-arm trials of six drugs, no closed loop), contributed by the two aripiprazole–risperidone trials. Publication bias not assessable with six trials (funnel plots only); not downgraded, noted. Very low. Status single study: the claim rests on one network meta-analysis whose six trial reports have not been read. The trials test five different drug pairs (only aripiprazole against risperidone twice), the review reports only that each found no significant difference, not the direction of each result (METHODS §6.4 counts pooled trials when the review reports their direction), and the network's indirect differences come from one analysis; a run of non-significant results in small head-to-head trials is not a replicated finding. The two Chinese trials also share authors, and the narrative reviews describe some of the same trials, so they add no independent study. The olanzapine–haloperidol trial (Leelahanaj et al., 2005), probably the trial the narrative reviews describe as the 2009 Cochrane review's single trial with 58 participants, is listed in the network meta-analysis with 56 (29 and 27). Not yet read (built-in browser unavailable on 2026-10-17): the systematic reviews of Fluyau et al. (2019) and Hall et al. (2026), and the 24-month randomized trial of aripiprazole or paliperidone against treatment as usual (Chung et al., 2026), which the currency check of 2026-10-16 identifies as bearing on benefit beyond usual care.

set.plain: Three reviews found eight small, short trials of medicines for meth psychosis, about 500 people in all. Six compared one medicine with another and found no clear winner. Two small trials against a dummy pill, in people already improving, and one two-year trial against usual care favoured the medicine on some measures, but these trials have serious flaws. Nobody has studied stopping the medicine.
set.population: Adults with methamphetamine psychosis (two trials are titled as amphetamine psychosis), mostly inpatients and men, in trials in Thailand, Iran, China and Malaysia; one 24-month trial in Hong Kong of mostly mild stimulant-induced psychosis (methamphetamine or cocaine), 17% with an earlier schizophrenia or schizoaffective diagnosis
set.comparator: Another antipsychotic (six trials); placebo after the acute episode had largely settled (two trials); usual psychiatric care, which often included another antipsychotic (one trial)
set.outcome: Severity of psychotic symptoms after 3 to 12 weeks; clinicians' global ratings at 12 and 24 months (one trial); dropout; side effects; relapse after stopping (no data)
set.magnitude: Six head-to-head randomized trials (searches to June 2020), 395 participants, 42 to 120 per trial, 21 to 42 days; no placebo arm. Network estimates against risperidone, main symptoms at the end of treatment (SMD of final values, not of change scores): olanzapine −1.09 (−1.89 to −0.28) and quetiapine −0.86 (−1.61 to −0.11), indirect only; haloperidol −0.60 (−1.20 to 0.01), paliperidone extended-release −0.33 (−0.69 to 0.03) and aripiprazole 0.27 (−0.13 to 0.68), direct. Aripiprazole against olanzapine 1.36 (0.46 to 2.26), quetiapine 1.13 (0.28 to 1.98), haloperidol 0.87 (0.14 to 1.60) and paliperidone extended-release 0.60 (0.06 to 1.14), indirect. No direct comparison significant. Dropout odds ratios against risperidone 0.18 to 2.77, every interval including 1. Authors' GRADE: low or very low for every estimate. Two further systematic reviews share these trials (searches to November 2018: 6 trials, 314 participants; to March 2026: 8 trials, 514 participants) and add two placebo-controlled trials after the acute episode: aripiprazole, 8 weeks, 37 participants, between-group p = 0.032; paliperidone extended-release, 12 weeks, 80 participants, p = 0.006, lost to follow-up 28% vs 55% (OR 0.31, 0.12 to 0.79). Within-arm changes from baseline in the 4-week trials d = 3.4 to 5.5 (not treatment effects). Usual-care trial (165 participants, 24 months): CGI-S change against usual care at 12 months aripiprazole −0.55 (−1.03 to −0.07), d −0.31, paliperidone −0.40 (−0.86 to 0.06); at 24 months, unblinded, −0.65 (−1.22 to −0.09) and −0.02 (−0.60 to 0.56); BPRS-24 no consistent difference; 70% assessed at 12 months, 54% at 24 months; registered primary outcome (relapse over 36 months) not reported. Side effects, trial level as tabulated by the 2026 review: extrapyramidal symptoms 15 of 29 on haloperidol vs 0 of 29 on olanzapine (OR 63.07, 3.52 to 1129.74); discontinuation for adverse effects 7 of 21 on aripiprazole vs 0 of 21 on risperidone (OR 22.24, 1.18 to 420.39).
set.grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence, read through three systematic reviews that share their trials (Srisurapanont et al., 2021, a network meta-analysis, AMSTAR 2 low confidence; Fluyau et al., 2019, critically low; Hall et al., 2026, low) and one trial against usual care read in full together with its registry record (Chung et al., 2026; RoB 2 high); the eight shorter trial reports themselves have not been read. Starts high. Risk of bias −1: two of the six head-to-head trials were open-label and allocation concealment was unclear in four; both indirect advantages over risperidone, and three of the four against aripiprazole, are chained through the open-label haloperidol–risperidone pilot trial (44 participants); the two placebo-controlled trials are known only through reviews that describe their analyses inconsistently; and the usual-care trial changed its primary outcome after the data were collected, lost 30% of assessments at 12 months and 46% at 24 months, and rated its second year unblinded. Taken alone, the comparison with usual care would be rated down two levels for risk of bias; certainty would be very low either way. Indirectness −1: the network is a chain without a closed loop, so every indirect estimate rests on transitivity, which the authors themselves doubt (participants and designs differ); two trials are titled as amphetamine psychosis; the placebo-controlled trials enrolled people whose symptoms had largely settled; the usual-care trial included cocaine-induced psychosis and 17% with an earlier schizophrenia or schizoaffective diagnosis, and its usual care included antipsychotics for most participants by 24 months. No trial compares an antipsychotic with none during an acute episode, the claim's open question. Imprecision −2: 37 to 120 participants per short trial, every direct head-to-head interval includes no difference, dropout odds ratios have intervals as wide as 0.00 to 218, and the usual-care trial's 12-month CGI-S difference (−0.55, −1.03 to −0.07) comes from 116 people assessed. Inconsistency not downgraded, though it can hardly be judged: the network's global I² of 0% for main symptoms rests on one degree of freedom (six two-arm trials of six drugs, no closed loop), contributed by the two aripiprazole–risperidone trials; the three reviews read one aripiprazole–risperidone trial (Farnia et al., 2014) in different directions; and in the usual-care trial the global ratings and the symptom ratings disagree. Publication bias not assessable with so few trials; not downgraded, noted. Very low. The network estimates are differences in end-of-treatment scores (the review used final values for all symptom analyses), not in how much symptoms fell. Status mixed (changed from single study, which rested on there being one network meta-analysis): the three reviews share their trials and count once (METHODS §6.3), but the claim now also rests on three trials against placebo or usual care from three independent groups (Malaysia, China, Hong Kong). The head-to-head trials test five different drug pairs and their directions are reported inconsistently across the reviews; the trials against placebo or usual care favour the antipsychotic on some outcomes but not on others (the usual-care trial's symptom ratings; paliperidone at 24 months), in different populations and with serious flaws, and no explanation has been tested. Counting direction alone, the three trials against placebo or usual care would meet the definition of replicated; this reader judges mixed the more accurate label because their populations, outcomes and risk of bias differ. The two Chinese head-to-head trials share authors, and the narrative reviews describe some of the same trials. The olanzapine–haloperidol trial (Leelahanaj et al., 2005), probably the trial the narrative reviews describe as the 2009 Cochrane review's single trial with 58 participants, is listed with 58 (29 and 29) by the 2019 and 2026 reviews and with 56 (29 and 27) by the network meta-analysis. The placebo-controlled aripiprazole trial (Sulaiman et al., 2013) may have randomized people after an open-label aripiprazole phase reported in a dissertation (Sulaiman, 2011): that phase's end PANSS (51.6) equals the trial's entry PANSS in the network meta-analysis (editors' inference; the trial report has not been read).

grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Open-label head-to-head trials and unclear allocation concealment; placebo-controlled trials seen only through reviews; the usual-care trial changed its primary outcome after data collection and lost 30–46% of assessments (alone it would be rated down two levels).

grade.domains.indirectness.note: Indirect network estimates rest on transitivity; placebo-controlled trials enrolled people already improving; the usual-care trial included cocaine psychosis, 17% with earlier schizophrenia, and usual care that mostly included antipsychotics; no acute-phase comparison with no antipsychotic.

grade.domains.imprecision.note: 37 to 120 participants per short trial; no direct head-to-head interval excludes no difference; the usual-care trial's CGI-S interval (−1.03 to −0.07) rests on 116 people assessed.

Head-to-head randomized evidence on antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis, as identified by a systematic review and network meta-analysis with searches to June 2020 and by two other systematic reviews that contain the same trials (searches to November 2018: five of the six; to March 2026: all six), consists of six small, short (21 to 42 days), single-site trials
Each trial reported no significant difference between its two drugs on the main psychotic symptoms, and the trials were too small to show that the drugs work equally well.

The network meta-analysis reports that each trial found no significant difference between its two drugs on the main psychotic symptoms (the 2026 review instead gives one aripiprazole–risperidone trial a between-group p < 0.001 on positive symptoms, and the 2019 review describes that trial in both directions), and the trials were too small to show that the drugs work equally well.

Because no trial had a placebo arm, these trials cannot show whether antipsychotics speed recovery beyond what abstinence alone achieves; the one placebo-controlled trial the review found, of aripiprazole in people whose psychotic symptoms had already subsided, was excluded.

Because none of these trials had a placebo arm, they cannot show whether antipsychotics speed recovery beyond what abstinence alone achieves; symptoms fell steeply in every arm, but the large effect sizes the other two reviews report (d = 3.4 to 5.5 in the 4-week trials) are changes from baseline within each arm, which cannot separate a drug effect from recovery with abstinence and time. Two small placebo-controlled trials, which the network meta-analysis did not include, enrolled people whose symptoms had already largely settled: aripiprazole for 8 weeks in 37 outpatients (symptoms fell more than on placebo, between-group p = 0.032) and paliperidone extended-release for 12 weeks in 80 people stabilized on drug-treatment wards before discharge (reported as favouring paliperidone, p = 0.006; 28% against 55% lost to follow-up); they bear on continued treatment after the acute episode rather than on its treatment. The only trial against usual care (Hong Kong, 2026; 165 people with stimulant-induced psychosis, about nine in ten of whom had used methamphetamine, mostly mildly ill) randomized them to aripiprazole, paliperidone or usual care, in which 55% were antipsychotic-free at randomization and 24% at 24 months. On clinicians' global severity ratings (CGI-S), aripiprazole improved more than usual care at 12 months (−0.55 points, 95% CI −1.03 to −0.07; d −0.31) and at 24 months, when ratings were no longer blind; paliperidone did not differ; and symptom ratings (BPRS-24) showed no consistent difference. That trial's registered primary outcome, relapse over 36 months, was changed after the trial ended, first to the BPRS-24 and then to the global ratings it reports; 17% of its participants had an earlier diagnosis of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, which the registry lists as an exclusion, and without them the 12-month CGI-S difference was not significant (p = 0.12); only 54% were assessed at 24 months. No trial has followed people after the antipsychotic was stopped, so how long to treat and the risk of relapse after stopping are unstudied.
Side effects were not pooled; as narrative reviews describe it, the one trial included in a 2009 Cochrane review found fewer extrapyramidal side effects on olanzapine than on haloperidol.

Side effects were not pooled; as the 2026 review tabulates them, extrapyramidal symptoms occurred in 15 of 29 participants on haloperidol and none of 29 on olanzapine in the olanzapine–haloperidol trial (probably the single trial of the 2009 Cochrane review that narrative reviews describe), 10 against 2 stopped early, and in one aripiprazole–risperidone trial 7 of 21 on aripiprazole and none of 21 on risperidone stopped because of adverse effects; in the usual-care trial, serious adverse events were one suicide in the aripiprazole arm and three paliperidone discontinuations (atrial fibrillation, QTc prolongation, acute renal failure with pneumonia).

expect.statement: In a systematic review of studies of methamphetamine-associated psychosis to March 2018, mostly of hospital patients and without appraisal of study quality, 27 studies reported the share of participants still psychotic more than a month after stopping use: the median study reported 25%, ranging from none in six laboratory studies in which volunteers were given the drug (symptoms resolved within 12 hours to 7 days) to 96%, with a median of 40% in longitudinal studies; Japanese studies reported more persistence (median 44%) than studies elsewhere (12%), which the review's authors attribute to the ICD rule allowing psychosis to last up to 6 months before a primary psychotic disorder is diagnosed, although only about a third of the Japanese studies (35%, against 6% elsewhere) used ICD-10. Second-hand reports of hospital series add 27% and 17% still psychotic beyond one and three months despite abstinence and antipsychotic treatment in 104 Japanese inpatients (cited by the systematic review); 16% and 17% after 1 and 3 months of abstinence in two reports from one Taiwanese research group, probably on one sample (a systematic review combines them as one study population of 445), with the denominator not explained and conflicting statements on family history in the narrative review that quotes them; and 10–28% beyond 6 months (narrative reviews). Later schizophrenia diagnoses ranged from 5% (China, second-hand) to about 39% in a Thai cohort of more than 1,000 people after a first hospitalization, a figure three reviews give differently (38.8% at 5 years; nearly 40% within 6 years; and, if the systematic review's study of 1,116 people after a first hospitalization is the same cohort, 33–38% after 6–7 years together with a study of 28 people); the systematic review gives 16% within 16 years for a Finnish register study of 825 people, and a narrative review gives 19–30% for register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis. These figures cannot show whether methamphetamine caused a lasting illness or revealed an existing vulnerability, whether some first episodes were primary psychoses attributed to drug use, or whether some later diagnoses relabel a persistent methamphetamine psychosis, since one review notes that diagnostic rules call for a primary psychotic diagnosis once psychosis persists. Recurrence with renewed use is common in clinical series, and in one follow-up positive symptoms rose in former patients who resumed use; Japanese researchers, as one review reports, describe spontaneous relapses after remission, which stressful situations seem to trigger in susceptible people. None of these figures has been checked in the primary studies, and a 2020 meta-analysis of transition to schizophrenia has not yet been read.
expect.plain: Across 27 studies of meth-related psychosis, mostly in hospital patients, the typical study found 1 in 4 people still had symptoms over a month after stopping; studies ranged from none to almost all. About 1 in 20 to 2 in 5 were later diagnosed with schizophrenia, which does not show meth caused it. Psychosis often returns with renewed use.
expect.magnitude: Systematic review, 27 studies with duration data: median 25% still psychotic beyond one month (laboratory studies 0%; longitudinal studies median 40%, range 14–96%; Japanese studies median 44%, range 18–96%, against 12%, range 0–39%, elsewhere; t = 4.79, p = .0001); case reports 2 of 24. Later schizophrenia diagnosis: 33–38% after 6–7 years (two studies, 1116 and 28 people); 16% within 16 years (825 people). Second-hand in narrative reviews: 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months (one research group, probably one sample); beyond 6 months 10–28%; later schizophrenia 5.0% (China) to 38.8% at 5 years (Thailand; nearly 40% within 6 years in another review); 19.1–30% in register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis. Japanese inpatient series cited by the systematic review: 27% beyond one month, 17% beyond three months (n=104). No pooled estimate or interval.
expect.population: People with methamphetamine-associated psychosis, mostly hospitalized
expect.grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim (base rates of persistence and of later diagnosis); observational, starts low. The claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews: a systematic review read in full (Voce et al., 2019; AMSTAR 2 critically low on the first reading) now supports the persistence and transition figures, although it reports them second-hand from primary studies it did not appraise, as unweighted medians without intervals. Risk of bias −1: mostly hospital samples, abstinence not verified, antipsychotic treatment and polydrug use not accounted for, and a median that includes six laboratory studies of volunteers given the drug, which observed no persistence (symptoms resolved within 12 hours to 7 days). Inconsistency −1: persistence ranges from 0% to 96% across studies, which the review's authors attribute to diagnostic rules (median 44% in Japanese studies against 12% elsewhere), although only 35% of the Japanese studies used ICD-10 (25% DSM-IV; elsewhere 6% and 42%), so the explanation covers about a third of them at most and is untested; later schizophrenia diagnosis ranges from 5% to about 39%, the Thai figure and its follow-up are reported differently by three reviews, and the Finnish register study appears as 16% within 16 years in the systematic review while a narrative review gives 19–30% for register studies. Very low. Status mixed: persistence beyond a month ranges from 0% to 96%, and the review's partial explanations (laboratory against clinical designs; Japanese against other studies) leave a wide unexplained spread within groups (18–96% in Japan, 0–39% elsewhere); later schizophrenia diagnoses run from 5% to about 39%. The inconsistency is in size, not in whether persistence occurs in clinical samples. Not yet read (built-in browser unavailable on 2026-10-17): the 2020 meta-analysis of transition from substance-induced psychoses to schizophrenia (Murrie et al.), which should replace the second-hand transition figures, and the register cohorts the currency check of 2026-10-16 lists.

set.plain: Across 27 studies of meth-related psychosis, mostly in hospital patients, the typical study found 1 in 4 people still had symptoms over a month after stopping; studies ranged from none to almost all. A 2020 review found that about 1 in 5 people with amphetamine-type psychosis were later diagnosed with schizophrenia, with figures varying widely between studies; this does not show meth caused it. Psychosis often returns with renewed use.
set.magnitude: Systematic review, 27 studies with duration data: median 25% still psychotic beyond one month (laboratory studies 0%; longitudinal studies median 40%, range 14–96%; Japanese studies median 44%, range 18–96%, against 12%, range 0–39%, elsewhere; t = 4.79, p = .0001); case reports 2 of 24. Later schizophrenia diagnosis, meta-analysis (searches to 2018): amphetamines 22% (95% CI 14–34%), 5 estimates, 2284 people, I² 96%; all substance-induced psychoses 25% (18–35%), 25 studies, 34,224 people, I² 99%; cannabis 34% (25–46%); alcohol 9% (6–15%); no significant moderator. Systematic review: 33–38% after 6–7 years (two studies, 1116 and 28 people; the meta-analysis lists the Thai cohort as 39% after 5 years with 40% followed up); 16% within 16 years (825 people). Randomized treatment trial, Hong Kong: 7 of 137 (5.1%) within 24 months. Second-hand in narrative reviews: 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months (one research group, probably one sample); beyond 6 months 10–28%; later schizophrenia 5.0% (China) to 38.8% at 5 years (Thailand; nearly 40% within 6 years in another review); 19.1–30% in register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis. Japanese inpatient series cited by the systematic review: 27% beyond one month, 17% beyond three months (n=104). No pooled estimate or interval for persistence.
set.population: People with methamphetamine-associated psychosis, mostly hospitalized (for later schizophrenia, also pooled cohorts of amphetamine-type substance-induced psychosis)
set.grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim (base rates of persistence and of later diagnosis); observational, starts low. The claim rests on a systematic review read in full (Voce et al., 2019; AMSTAR 2 critically low), which reports persistence and transition figures second-hand from primary studies it did not appraise, as unweighted medians without intervals, and now also on a meta-analysis of transition read in full (Murrie et al., 2020; AMSTAR 2 low confidence, provisional, on the first reading), which pools five estimates for amphetamine-type psychoses (22%, 14% to 34%) but does not name the studies and groups cocaine with methamphetamine and amphetamine as stimulants. Risk of bias −1: mostly hospital samples, abstinence not verified, antipsychotic treatment and polydrug use not accounted for, a persistence median that includes six laboratory studies of volunteers given the drug, which observed no persistence (symptoms resolved within 12 hours to 7 days), and transition figures from register or routine diagnoses with follow-up as incomplete as 40% (the Thai cohort). Inconsistency −1: persistence ranges from 0% to 96% across studies, which the review's authors attribute to diagnostic rules (median 44% in Japanese studies against 12% elsewhere), although only 35% of the Japanese studies used ICD-10 (25% DSM-IV; elsewhere 6% and 42%), so the explanation covers about a third of them at most and is untested; the pooled transition estimate for amphetamines carries an I² of 96%, unexplained by any moderator the meta-analysis tested, single studies range from 5% to about 39%, and the Thai cohort is reported four ways by four reviews. Indirectness not downgraded: the persistence figures concern methamphetamine; the pooled transition figure covers amphetamine-type psychoses and may include some cocaine psychoses, which the statement says. Imprecision not downgraded: the pooled interval (14% to 34%) is wide, but the claim describes a range. Very low. Status mixed: persistence beyond a month ranges from 0% to 96%, and the review's partial explanations (laboratory against clinical designs; Japanese against other studies) leave a wide unexplained spread within groups (18–96% in Japan, 0–39% elsewhere); later schizophrenia diagnoses run from 5% to about 39% in single studies, with a pooled 22% and I² 96%. The inconsistency is in size, not in whether persistence or later diagnosis occurs in clinical samples. The meta-analysis and the systematic review share at least three studies (the Thai cohort, a small prospective amphetamine cohort and the Finnish register study), so they are not independent. The 5.1% within 24 months comes from a treated trial sample that included cocaine-induced psychosis and excluded, after the fact, 28 people with an earlier diagnosis. Not yet read: the register cohorts the currency check of 2026-10-16 lists.

grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Mostly hospital samples with unverified abstinence and untreated confounding by medication and other drugs; transition from register or routine diagnoses with follow-up as low as 40%.

grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Persistence 0% to 96% across studies, only partly explained; transition I² 96% for amphetamines in the meta-analysis, single studies 5% to about 39%.

grade.domains.indirectness.note: Not downgraded; the pooled transition figure covers amphetamine-type psychoses and may include some cocaine psychoses.

replace: Later schizophrenia diagnoses ranged from 5% (China, second-hand) to about 39% in a Thai cohort of more than 1,000 people after a first hospitalization, a figure three reviews give differently (38.8% at 5 years; nearly 40% within 6 years; and, if the systematic review's study of 1,116 people after a first hospitalization is the same cohort, 33–38% after 6–7 years together with a study of 28 people); the systematic review gives 16% within 16 years for a Finnish register study of 825 people, and a narrative review gives 19–30% for register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis.

A 2020 meta-analysis of cohorts of substance-induced psychosis (searches 1980 to 2018, English only) pooled five estimates for amphetamine-type psychoses, 2,284 people: 22% (95% CI 14% to 34%) later received a diagnosis of schizophrenia, with extreme heterogeneity between studies (I² 96%); the five studies are not named in the article, and its methods group cocaine with methamphetamine and amphetamine as stimulants. Across all substance-induced psychoses the pooled figure was 25% (18% to 35%; 25 studies, I² 99%), highest after cannabis (34%) and lowest after alcohol (9%), and no study feature tested, including length and completeness of follow-up, significantly predicted it. Single-study figures range from 5% (China, second-hand) to about 39% in a Thai cohort of 1,116 people with methamphetamine psychosis after a first hospitalization, which four reviews report four ways: 38.8% at 5 years, nearly 40% within 6 years, 33–38% after 6–7 years together with a small cohort of 28 people, and, in the meta-analysis, 39% after 5 years with only 40% of the cohort followed up. The 2019 systematic review gives 16% within 16 years for a Finnish register study of 825 people, a narrative review gives 19–30% for register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis, and in a 24-month randomized treatment trial in Hong Kong 7 of 137 people (5.1%) with stimulant-induced psychosis and no earlier diagnosis were newly diagnosed with schizophrenia.
None of these figures has been checked in the primary studies, and a 2020 meta-analysis of transition to schizophrenia has not yet been read.
None of the single-study figures has been checked in the primary studies.

evidence_add.extracted: The five amphetamine estimates are not identified in the article, and the methods record methamphetamine, amphetamine and cocaine psychoses together as stimulant-induced. No study feature predicted transition at the review's threshold of P < .01 (length of follow-up P = .3433; percentage followed up β −1.716, P = .0785, lower transition with more complete follow-up; older cohorts lower, P = .0286). Few studies recorded the amount of use before the episode, comorbid substance use disorders or continued use; most diagnoses came from registers or routine care (research interviews in 8 studies, 127 people). The authors state that substance-induced is used by convention, not as a presumed causal link.
